grammar.prompt: You learned the information too late to tell your friend. Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: If I would have known, I would have told you.
If I had known, I would have told you.
grammar.answer: If I had known, I would have told you.
grammar.explanation: Use had + past participle in the if-clause, not would have.

grammar.title: Present Perfect with 'Ever' (Life Experiences)
grammar.rule: Structure: have / has + past participle. Use 'ever' in questions to ask about life experiences at any time.
grammar.prompt: Have you ______ visited a film studio in another country?
grammar.explanation: 'Ever' is used in questions asking about life experiences in the Present Perfect.

grammar.title: Superlatives with 'By far'
grammar.rule: Structure: by far + the + superlative adjective. Used to say something is clearly the best.
grammar.prompt: Many critics say that this new drama is by far ______ film of the year.
grammar.explanation: 'By far' comes before 'the + superlative adjective' to add strong emphasis.

grammar.title: Causative Verbs: Let + Object + Base Verb
grammar.rule: The verb 'let' means to allow someone to do something. It is followed by an object and a base verb without 'to'.
grammar.prompt: The security team did not ______ the photographer enter the backstage door.
grammar.explanation: 'Let' is followed by an object and a base verb ('enter') without 'to'.

grammar.title: Gerunds after 'Good at'
grammar.rule: After preposition phrases like 'good at', always use a verb ending in -ing (a gerund).
grammar.prompt: She has practiced art for years and is very good at ______ small clay bowls.
grammar.explanation: Prepositions like 'at' in 'good at' must be followed by a verb ending in '-ing'.

grammar.title: Wishes about the Past (Wish + Past Perfect)
grammar.rule: Use 'wish + had + past participle' to talk about regrets about things that happened in the past.
grammar.prompt: The actor wishes he ______ taken that movie role before the auditions ended.
grammar.explanation: To express regret about something in the past, use 'wish + had + past participle'.

grammar.title: Polite Requests with 'Will you?'
grammar.rule: You can add 'will you?' at the end of an instruction or command to turn it into a polite request.
grammar.prompt: Please turn down the TV volume a little, ______ you?
grammar.explanation: 'Will you?' is added to the end of a command to make it a polite request.

grammar.title: Third Conditional: If + Past Perfect
grammar.rule: Structure: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle. Used to imagine a different past.
grammar.prompt: If the journalist ______ checked the facts, the paper would not have printed the mistake.
grammar.explanation: In the 'if' part of a Third Conditional sentence, use 'had + past participle'.

grammar.title: Present Perfect with 'Never' (Life Experiences)
grammar.rule: Use 'never' between have/has and the past participle to say you have not had an experience in your life.
grammar.prompt: The young director has ______ worked on such a big movie project before.
grammar.explanation: 'Never' is placed between 'has' and the past participle 'worked' to show an experience has not happened.

grammar.title: Causative Verbs: Allow + Object + To-Infinitive
grammar.rule: Unlike 'let', the verb 'allow' requires an object followed by a verb with 'to' (allow someone to do something).
grammar.prompt: The studio rules do not allow visitors ______ photos during the recording.
grammar.explanation: The verb 'allow' is followed by an object and 'to' + verb ('to take').

grammar.title: Causative Verbs: Make + Object + Base Verb
grammar.rule: When 'make' means forcing someone to do something, it takes an object and a base verb without 'to'.
grammar.prompt: The strict boss made the team ______ the work until it was completely right.
grammar.explanation: The verb 'make' is followed by an object and a base verb ('repeat') without 'to'.

grammar.title: Gerunds after 'Bad at'
grammar.rule: After 'bad at', always use a verb ending in -ing (a gerund).
grammar.prompt: He likes watching sports on TV, but he admits he is quite bad at ______ tennis.
grammar.explanation: After the phrase 'bad at', use the '-ing' verb form ('playing').

grammar.title: Wishes for Change (Wish + Would)
grammar.rule: Use 'wish + would' when you want another person to stop doing something annoying.
grammar.prompt: The singer wishes the photographers ______ stop waiting outside her front gate.
grammar.explanation: Use 'wish + would' when you want someone else to change their behavior.

grammar.title: Third Conditional: Would (not) have
grammar.rule: In the result part of a Third Conditional sentence, use 'would (not) have + past participle'.
grammar.prompt: If the actor had worn a helmet for the jump, he ______ hurt his head.
grammar.explanation: In the result part of a Third Conditional, use 'would not have + past participle'.

grammar.title: Superlatives with 'By far' (The Worst)
grammar.rule: Use 'by far + the worst' to emphasize that something is clearly the lowest in quality.
grammar.prompt: Reviewers agreed that the second movie was by far ______ part of the series.
grammar.explanation: 'By far' adds strong emphasis before 'the worst' to show an extreme comparison.

grammar.title: Future Simple with 'Will'
grammar.rule: Use will + base verb to talk about future actions, decisions, and promises.
grammar.prompt: I am very hungry, so I ______ make a sandwich for lunch.
grammar.explanation: Use 'will' before a base verb ('make') to talk about a future decision.

grammar.title: Purpose with 'So That'
grammar.rule: Use 'so that' followed by can or could to explain the reason or purpose behind an action.
grammar.prompt: Mona drinks warm milk before bed ______ she can sleep well.
grammar.explanation: Use 'so that' followed by 'can' to explain the purpose of an action.

grammar.title: Relative Pronoun 'Who' for People
grammar.rule: Use the relative pronoun 'who' to give information about a person.
grammar.prompt: The kind farmer ______ grows fresh vegetables gave us a big basket of apples.
grammar.explanation: Use 'who' to refer to a person ('The kind farmer').

grammar.title: Past Simple Questions with 'Did'
grammar.rule: Use 'Did + subject + base verb' to ask questions about finished past actions.
grammar.prompt: ______ you eat breakfast before coming to school this morning?
grammar.explanation: Use 'Did' at the start of a past simple question followed by a base verb ('eat').

grammar.prompt: My younger brother prefers to study in his bedroom by ______ without any help from our parents.
grammar.rule: Use 'by + reflexive pronoun' (myself, himself, herself, ourselves) to show that someone does an action alone without help.
grammar.explanation: 'Himself' is the correct reflexive pronoun for a male singular subject ('My younger brother') when expressing that he studies alone.

grammar.prompt: Karim is very friendly, but he is not as ______ as his outgoing twin brother.
grammar.rule: Use 'as + base adjective + as' (or 'not as + base adjective + as') to compare two people. The adjective remains in its simple base form without adding '-er' or 'more'.
grammar.explanation: The adjective between 'as ... as' must remain in its base form ('confident') without comparative markers.

grammar.prompt: ______ quality time with close friends on weekends helps reduce work stress.
grammar.rule: Use a gerund (verb + -ing) when the verb functions as the grammatical subject of the sentence.
grammar.explanation: 'Spending' is a gerund acting as the subject of the sentence, followed by the singular verb 'helps'.

grammar.prompt: If my best friend ______ closer to my neighborhood, we would see each other every evening.
grammar.rule: In the second conditional for imaginary present situations, use the Past Simple in the 'if' clause and 'would + base verb' in the main clause.
grammar.explanation: 'Lived' is the Past Simple verb required in the 'if' condition to describe an unreal or unlikely present situation.

grammar.prompt: Mona and I ______ be inseparable classmates in primary school, but now we rarely talk.
grammar.rule: Use 'used to + base verb' to talk about past habits or states of being that are no longer true in the present.
grammar.explanation: 'Used to' describes a past state of close friendship that has ended or changed over time.

grammar.prompt: After moving into a new apartment, it took Omar several months to get used to ______ with a roommate.
grammar.rule: Use 'get used to + gerund (verb + -ing)' to describe the ongoing process of becoming accustomed to a new situation.
grammar.explanation: The phrase 'get used to' must be followed by a noun or gerund with '-ing' ('living').

grammar.prompt: My grandfather is much ______ than my father, but he still takes daily morning walks.
grammar.rule: For short one-syllable adjectives, add '-er' to form the comparative adjective before 'than'.
grammar.explanation: 'Old' is a single-syllable adjective, so its regular comparative form before 'than' is 'older' (not 'more old').

grammar.prompt: Which sentence describes possession?
grammar.explanation: Use the simple form for possession. Some verbs can be continuous when they express an action.

grammar.prompt: Which sentence correctly describes an activity happening now?
options: I am own a house now.
I am believing this fact now.
I am knowing the answer now.
grammar.explanation: Having lunch is an activity. The continuous is possible for this action sense.

grammar.prompt: Complete: Please wait; I ______ about your question.
grammar.explanation: Active thought can be an action in progress. I think it is good instead expresses an opinion.

grammar.prompt: Complete: I ______ swim now, but I could not swim as a child.
grammar.explanation: Can expresses present ability; could can express general past ability.

grammar.prompt: Complete: When she was six, she ______ already read simple books.
grammar.explanation: Could expresses a general ability in the past.

grammar.prompt: Which question makes a polite request?
options: Could you close the door, please?
Could you closed the door, please?
Could you closing the door, please?
Could you to close the door, please?
grammar.answer: Could you close the door, please?
grammar.explanation: After could, use the base verb. Could you is a polite request; Can you can also be polite.

grammar.prompt: Mona called Ali. Ask about the person who made the call.
grammar.explanation: Who is the subject, so a positive past-simple question does not add did.

grammar.prompt: Mona called Ali. Ask about the person who received the call.
grammar.explanation: Use did plus the base verb in this object question. Whom is a formal object form.

grammar.prompt: Choose the formal question with the preposition first.
grammar.explanation: Whom is the formal object form after a preposition. Who did you eat with? is common in everyday English.

grammar.prompt: The bottle is below the table. Complete: It is ______ the table.
grammar.explanation: Under describes a lower position.

grammar.prompt: Complete: We walked ______ the neighbourhood to explore its different streets.
grammar.explanation: Around can describe movement through different parts of an area.

grammar.prompt: Complete: He will come ______ seven in the evening.
grammar.explanation: Back expresses return; at introduces a clock time.

grammar.prompt: Complete: I attend classes ______ English.
grammar.explanation: Use to plus the base verb to state the purpose of attending.

grammar.prompt: Complete: This brush is ______ the floor.
grammar.explanation: For plus -ing can describe the function of an object.

grammar.prompt: Complete: We stayed inside ______ it was raining.
grammar.explanation: Because introduces a clause giving a reason.

grammar.prompt: Choose the usual location phrases.
options: arrive in Cairo; arrive at the station
arrive at Cairo; arrive in the station
arrive to Cairo; arrive to the station
arrive on Cairo; arrive under the station
grammar.answer: arrive in Cairo; arrive at the station
grammar.explanation: Cities and countries normally take in; a station treated as a destination point normally takes at. It is not a physical-size rule.

grammar.prompt: Complete the general preference: I ______ reading travel books.
grammar.explanation: Like plus -ing can describe a general preference.

grammar.prompt: Complete the polite wish: I would like ______ a room.
grammar.explanation: Would like takes to plus the base verb for this wish.

grammar.prompt: Complete: Every evening, I ______ the dishes.
grammar.explanation: Do the dishes is the usual fixed expression.

grammar.prompt: Complete: Before shopping, she ______ a list.
grammar.explanation: Make a list is the usual expression; she takes makes in the present simple.

grammar.prompt: Complete: The kind message made me ______ happy.
grammar.explanation: In this active construction, make plus an object takes the base verb.

grammar.prompt: Complete: Open the car door and get ______ the car.
grammar.explanation: Use get in a car or taxi.

grammar.prompt: Complete: When the taxi stops, get ______ it.
grammar.explanation: The full exit expression is get out of a car or taxi.

grammar.prompt: Complete: I get ______ the bus here and get off at the next stop.
grammar.explanation: Use get on and get off with buses. This is a usage pattern, not a rule based only on size.

grammar.prompt: Complete: She got ______ her bike and started pedalling.
grammar.explanation: Use get on a bike, even though a bike is small.

grammar.prompt: Complete: How ______ chairs do we need?
grammar.explanation: Chairs is a plural countable noun, so use many.

grammar.prompt: Complete: How ______ furniture can fit here?
grammar.explanation: Furniture is uncountable, so use much.

grammar.prompt: Complete: We have ______ chairs, enough for three guests.
grammar.explanation: A few means some and modifies a plural countable noun.

grammar.prompt: Which sentence says there is almost no money and this is a problem?
options: We have a little money left.
We have a few money left.
grammar.explanation: Little stresses not enough; a little means some. Money is uncountable.

grammar.prompt: Which sentence uses a lot of correctly?
options: We bought a lot of furniture.
We bought a lot of furnitures.
We bought a lots of furniture.
grammar.answer: We bought a lot of furniture.
grammar.explanation: A lot of works with uncountable nouns and plural countable nouns. Furniture stays uncountable.

grammar.prompt: Complete: Look! Sara ______ the floor right now.
grammar.explanation: Use is plus the -ing form with Sara.

grammar.prompt: Complete: The children ______ television at the moment.
grammar.explanation: Use are not plus the -ing form with a plural subject.

grammar.prompt: Complete: I ______ on my phone right now.
grammar.explanation: Use am not plus the -ing form with I.

puns.joke: Some people seem to be built backwards: their noses run and their feet smell!
puns.pair: Running or smelling in ordinary bodily actions ↔ A dripping nose or feet giving off an odour

puns.joke: I used to be addicted to soap, but I am clean now!
puns.pair: Free of dirt ↔ No longer using an addictive substance

puns.joke: Why could the bicycle not stand on its own? It was two-tired!
puns.pair: Too tired to stand ↔ Having two tyres

puns.joke: If towels could tell jokes, they would have a dry sense of humor.
puns.pair: Not wet ↔ A serious-sounding style of humour

challenges.prompt:
Three people with strong work experience reached the final interview. The director ignored their results and gave the job to his nephew, who had not taken the required test. The family relationship decided the choice.

What does this situation show?
challenges.explanation: Nepotism means unfairly favoring a family member for a job or other advantage.

challenges.prompt:
Salma's manager wanted an update every fifteen minutes. He chose every small email detail and would not let her send anything before he checked it. She could make almost no work decisions herself.

What workplace problem is this?
challenges.explanation: Micromanagement is too much control over another person's small work decisions.

challenges.prompt:
Omar compares prices, repairs useful items, and plans his shopping. He buys good shoes when he needs them, but never spends just to look important. He wants to avoid waste, not refuse every cost.

Which word best describes him?
challenges.explanation: Frugal describes careful spending without waste. It does not mean refusing all necessary spending.

challenges.prompt:
A customer asked Mariam for a simple report by Friday. She finished on Thursday and added a short guide so the customer could use it easily. That extra help was not required.

Which idiom describes what she did?
challenges.explanation: Go the extra mile means do more than is expected to help or succeed.

challenges.prompt:
The club event cost 80,000 pounds. Ticket sales brought in exactly 80,000 pounds. The club paid every cost but had no extra money left.

Which idiom describes the result?
options: Save money for a rainy day
challenges.explanation: Break even means income exactly covers costs, with no profit or loss.

challenges.prompt:
Every payday, Hala puts a small amount aside for unexpected problems. When her fridge breaks, she can pay for the repair without asking anyone for money.

Which idiom describes her habit?
options: Save money for a rainy day
challenges.answer: Save money for a rainy day
linkedWords: Save money for a rainy day
challenges.explanation: Save money for a rainy day means keep money for a future problem or emergency.

challenges.prompt:
The team leader chose the wrong date for a project. When it failed, he told his bosses that a newer worker had chosen the date alone. He placed the blame on that worker to protect himself.

Which idiom describes his action?
challenges.explanation: Throw someone under the bus means blame or harm another person for your own protection.

challenges.prompt: When would someone naturally say, “Worth a shot”?
options: Before trying for a job even though you may not succeed
After learning that a coworker has lost their job
When saying a service is better than all others
After blaming a teammate to protect yourself
challenges.answer: Before trying for a job even though you may not succeed
challenges.explanation: Worth a shot means the possible benefit makes an attempt reasonable, even when success is not certain.

challenges.prompt: In which situation would someone naturally say, "Bite the bullet"?
options: Finally making the unpleasant call you have avoided all week
Admiring an actor who looks beautiful on screen
Describing someone who can do many kinds of practical work
Saying that an old laptop is no longer in good condition
challenges.answer: Finally making the unpleasant call you have avoided all week
challenges.explanation: Bite the bullet means stop avoiding an unpleasant but necessary action and make yourself do it.

challenges.prompt: Three items relate to borrowed money or security for it. Which one is different?

relationship.kind: borrowed money and security for it

challenges.explanation: Loan and mortgage are borrowed money; collateral is a guarantee that the money will be paid back. Refund is a returned payment, not part of that group.

challenges.prompt: Three words describe unfriendly or attacking behaviour. Which word is different?
challenges.explanation: Aggressive, hostile, and mean describe unfriendly behaviour. Timid describes a lack of courage or belief in yourself, not unkindness.

challenges.prompt: Freshman, Sophomore, Junior: which word completes the year labels in a four-year US college course?

relationship.kind: year labels in a four-year US college course

challenges.explanation: Senior is the fourth-year label in this system. Dean and tutor are roles, and campus is a place.

challenges.prompt: Put the words in order to make a correct sentence.
challenges.answer: A good manager never talks down to the staff.
challenges.explanation: Talk down to means speak as if the listener is less intelligent. A good manager is singular, so use talks.

challenges.prompt: Complete the sentence: The bank accepted the house as ______ in case the borrowed money was not paid back.
challenges.explanation: Collateral is valuable property offered as a guarantee when money is borrowed.

challenges.prompt: Write one sentence using both Loan and Collateral. The game checks only that the words appear, so compare your meaning and grammar with the example afterwards.
challenges.exampleAnswer: The bank gave her a loan after accepting her house as collateral.
challenges.explanation: The example connects the borrowed money with the property offered as security. Including both words alone does not prove the grammar or meaning is correct.

challenges.prompt: Write one sentence using Frugal and Budget. The automatic check only looks for the words; use the example to review your own sentence.
challenges.exampleAnswer: Her frugal habits helped her stay within her monthly budget.
challenges.explanation: The example links careful spending with a spending plan. Check your own grammar and meaning as well as the required words.

challenges.prompt:
Rewrite the sentence using “Call off” in the correct tense:
The manager cancelled the meeting because of the storm.
challenges.answer: The manager called off the meeting because of the storm.
acceptedAnswers: The manager called off the meeting because of the storm.
Because of the storm, the manager called off the meeting.
challenges.explanation: The past form is called off. With the full noun the meeting, the object can follow the phrase.

challenges.prompt: Rewrite using Let someone go in the past: The company ended his job at the end of the month.
challenges.answer: The company let him go at the end of the month.
acceptedAnswers: The company let him go at the end of the month.
challenges.explanation: Let stays let in the past. Put him between let and go: let him go.

challenges.prompt: Rewrite using Pass it off: He tried to hand the task to another worker instead of doing it himself.
challenges.answer: He tried to pass it off to another worker instead of doing it himself.
acceptedAnswers: He tried to pass it off to another worker instead of doing it himself.
Instead of doing it himself, he tried to pass it off to another worker.
challenges.explanation: In this task-transfer context, it stands for the task. Put it between pass and off.

challenges.prompt: Salma called the school and learned the trip time from a teacher. Which phrasal verb fits? She called to ______ when the trip would leave.
challenges.explanation: Find out means learn a fact. The other choices mean delay, meet by chance, or cancel.

challenges.prompt: Match each meaning to its phrasal verb.
challenges.explanation: The three questions test angry behaviour, seeking praise, and an unexpected meeting.

steps.prompt: Which phrase means suddenly attack someone with angry words or actions?
steps.explanation: Lash out describes a sudden angry attack.

steps.prompt: Which phrase means display things or abilities mainly to get praise?
steps.explanation: Show off describes trying to make people admire you.

steps.prompt: Which phrase means meet someone by chance?
steps.explanation: Run into describes an unplanned meeting.

challenges.prompt: Case file: “I didn't used to check the warranty.”
challenges.explanation: After didn't, use the base form: didn't use to.

steps.explanation: Didn't already marks the past. The next verb should be use.

steps.answer: I didn't use to check the warranty.
acceptedAnswers: I didn't use to check the warranty.

steps.explanation: Did marks the past, so the next verb stays in its base form.

challenges.prompt: Case file: "She is used to wake up early."
challenges.explanation: After be used to, use a noun or an -ing verb form. Here, use waking.

steps.explanation: The verb needs the -ing form after is used to.

steps.answer: She is used to waking up early.
acceptedAnswers: She is used to waking up early.
steps.explanation: Waking is the correct form after is used to.

steps.prompt: Why do we use waking here?
options: Be used to is followed by a noun or an -ing form
Used can only be followed by a base verb
steps.answer: Be used to is followed by a noun or an -ing form
steps.explanation: Be used to means the activity feels normal. It takes a noun or -ing form afterwards.

challenges.prompt: Case file: "If he had applied earlier, he would get the job." Both the application and its result are finished past events. Use the complete Third Conditional.
challenges.explanation: For this imagined past result, use would have got. A mixed conditional can have a different time meaning, but it is not the requested pattern.

steps.prompt: Is this a complete Third Conditional for a finished past result?
steps.explanation: Would get does not give the requested complete Third Conditional past-result form.

steps.prompt: Rewrite the full sentence as a complete Third Conditional about the past.
steps.answer: If he had applied earlier, he would have got the job.
acceptedAnswers: If he had applied earlier, he would have got the job.
If he had applied earlier, he would have gotten the job.
steps.explanation: Would have got and would have gotten are both accepted here.

options: if + past perfect, would have + past participle
if + past simple, would + base verb
if + past perfect, would + base verb
steps.answer: if + past perfect, would have + past participle
steps.explanation: The pattern imagines a different past situation and a different past result.

challenges.prompt: Case file: “I wish I saved more money last year.”
challenges.explanation: For something you wish had been different in a finished past year, use wish + past perfect.

steps.prompt: Does the sentence use the correct form for being sorry about a finished past year?
steps.explanation: Use had saved because last year is already finished.

steps.answer: I wish I had saved more money last year.
acceptedAnswers: I wish I had saved more money last year.
steps.explanation: Had saved describes the past action the speaker wishes had happened differently.

steps.prompt: Which meaning does this structure express?
steps.explanation: Wish + past perfect looks back at something the speaker cannot change now.

challenges.prompt: Mona bought a new vacuum for the carpet. What is the word doing here?
challenges.explanation: Here vacuum is a noun for the machine; in Please vacuum the carpet, it is a verb.

challenges.prompt: The iron is hot, so leave it on its stand. What does iron mean here?
options: A heated tool for smoothing clothes
challenges.answer: A heated tool for smoothing clothes
challenges.explanation: Iron is a noun for the tool here. In I iron my shirt, it is a verb.

challenges.prompt: Sara gave me a present on my birthday. Which meaning is used?
challenges.explanation: A present is a gift. Present your passport uses the verb meaning show or hand over.

challenges.prompt: Milk spilled onto the floor beneath the kitchen table. What does floor refer to?
challenges.explanation: Floor can name the walking surface or a building level. Here the spilled milk is on the surface.

challenges.prompt: The boat has a hole and may sink. Which meaning is used?
options: Go down below the water surface
Die from lack of air under water
challenges.answer: Go down below the water surface
challenges.explanation: Sink is a verb here. A boat can sink, but an object does not drown. The kitchen fixture is a noun sense.

challenges.prompt: They painted their own house. What does own add here?
challenges.explanation: Own follows their and stresses possession. They own the house uses own as a verb.

challenges.prompt: The doctor explained that the liver processes substances in the blood. Which sense is used?
challenges.explanation: Liver names an organ here. In a meal, it can also name that organ prepared as food.

challenges.prompt: Choose the usual British and American terms for the same city train system.
challenges.explanation: These are regional terms for the same taught transport concept, not different kinds of train.

challenges.prompt: A passenger has a break between two flights. Which statement is accurate in general English?
options: Both terms can describe this break
One always means exactly two hours
Neither term can describe air travel
challenges.answer: Both terms can describe this break
challenges.explanation: Layover and stopover overlap in general English. Do not infer a universal duration rule.

challenges.prompt: Which sentence correctly describes a completed decision yesterday?
options: Yesterday, I chose the shorter route.
Yesterday, I choose the shorter route.
Yesterday, I choice the shorter route.
Yesterday, I choosing the shorter route.
challenges.answer: Yesterday, I chose the shorter route.
challenges.explanation: Chose is past tense; choose is the base form; choice is a noun.

challenges.prompt: Which statement explains the relationship between the two expressions?
options: The longer expression names a specific use of the action
The shorter word means washing only
The longer phrase means removing wrinkles with heat
challenges.answer: The longer expression names a specific use of the action
challenges.explanation: Fold the clothes names a particular object of fold. Do not invent different actions.

challenges.prompt: A room is completely clean and everything is in its place. Which statement is fair?
options: Only one expression can ever describe a room
Neither expression concerns cleanliness or order
challenges.explanation: The meanings overlap. Spick and span particularly stresses thorough cleanliness.

challenges.prompt: Which statement distinguishes the place names correctly?
options: A platform is a boarding area within a station
Every railway station must be large
A platform is a whole city rail system
challenges.answer: A platform is a boarding area within a station
challenges.explanation: Station can mean a railway station in context; platform names the area beside the track.

challenges.prompt: A man becomes angry immediately over a tiny mistake but was cheerful a moment ago. Which description stresses quick anger?
challenges.explanation: Short-tempered stresses quick anger. Cranky and grumpy overlap in describing an irritable mood.

challenges.prompt: A stone falls below the water surface. Which statement is correct?
options: It can sink, but it cannot drown
It must drown before it can sink
Both words mean the same thing
Neither word can describe movement in water
challenges.answer: It can sink, but it cannot drown
challenges.explanation: Sink describes downward movement. Drown concerns being unable to breathe under water.

challenges.prompt: A woman owns a house and lets her sister live there with her. Which statement is correct?
options: Ownership and shared use can happen together
challenges.answer: Ownership and shared use can happen together
challenges.explanation: Own concerns possession; share concerns joint use or division.

challenges.prompt: Which description focuses on wrinkles being removed from fabric?
options: The shirt is smooth after pressing.
challenges.answer: The shirt is smooth after pressing.
challenges.explanation: Use smooth or uncreased for fabric with wrinkles removed; straight normally contrasts with bent or curved.

challenges.prompt: Which description places the two spaces correctly?
options: One is under the roof; the other is below ground
They are lexical opposites in every use
challenges.answer: One is under the roof; the other is below ground
challenges.explanation: Attic and basement name different house locations. A spatial contrast is not a general lexical antonym.

challenges.prompt: One bag stays above your seat; another travels in the hold. Which mapping is correct?
options: Both must stay in the cabin
Both names depend only on bag colour
challenges.explanation: The distinction concerns where bags travel; size limits vary by airline.

challenges.prompt: A driver collects a friend, leaves her at a hotel, then stops by the roadside. Which order names these actions?
options: Pick up; drop off; pull over
Drop off; pull over; pick up
Pull over; pick up; run over
Run over; drop off; hop on
challenges.answer: Pick up; drop off; pull over
challenges.explanation: Collecting, leaving a passenger and roadside stopping are different actions.

challenges.prompt: Which sentence is about losing a job rather than going to bed?
options: He may get the sack for missing work.
He will hit the sack after a tiring day.
challenges.answer: He may get the sack for missing work.
challenges.explanation: Get the sack means lose a job; hit the sack means go to bed.

challenges.prompt: Which statement about these food words is safest?
options: Their categories can overlap across cooking traditions
One is always sweet and the other always salty
Shape alone always determines the answer
challenges.answer: Their categories can overlap across cooking traditions
challenges.explanation: Use a clear dish or cooking context; long thin strips alone may fit either term.

challenges.prompt: Which description specifically points to a dresser?
options: A bedroom unit with drawers for clothes
An open platform outside an upper floor
A space just beneath the roof
A road divided by painted lines
challenges.answer: A bedroom unit with drawers for clothes
challenges.explanation: Drawers for clothes distinguish the dresser in this set; closet and cupboard uses can overlap.

challenges.prompt: Which sentence uses the adjective correctly?
challenges.explanation: Luxurious is an adjective; luxury is a noun. They are related forms, not opposites.

challenges.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses the adjective before a noun?
challenges.explanation: Cultural describes something related to a society's culture.

challenges.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses the quality noun?
options: Her being generously helped many families.
challenges.explanation: Generosity names the quality; generous describes a person.

challenges.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses the adjective?
challenges.explanation: Messy is an adjective; mess is a noun, as in The room is a mess.

challenges.prompt: Which sentence correctly describes the full train?
challenges.explanation: Crowded describes a place full of people. A crowd is a group of people.

challenges.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses the verb after will?
challenges.explanation: Use the base verb after will. Departure is the noun for leaving.

challenges.prompt: Which option is NOT a hotel job role in this set?
challenges.explanation: The first three can be hotel staff roles. A pedestrian is a person travelling on foot.
challenges.relationship: Hotel job roles versus a road user

challenges.prompt: Which option is NOT a vehicle control?
challenges.explanation: Three options are vehicle controls; dairy concerns milk products.
challenges.relationship: Vehicle controls versus a food category
